transcript:
Meeting Header
Date/Time: 2026-10-20 15:00 PDT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya Patel (Redwood AE), Jordan Kim (Redwood SE), Avery Cole (Redwood CSM), Elena Ruiz (CTO, CedarForge), Samir Patel (Infra), Priya Nair (ML Lead), Daniel Cho (Security)
Link to deck: https://redwood.example.com/decks/cedarforge-kickoff-deck (shared)
Runbook template: https://redwood.example.com/runbooks/template-activation (note)

[00:00] Maya Patel: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, appreciate the time. quick intros — i'll be the AE on the account, jordan's our systems engineer who will run the infra workshop, avery will help with adoption. elena, do you want to kick off from your side?

[00:22] Elena Ruiz: yeah thanks maya. hi all. cedarforge is excited to get this into staging. our priorities are pretty straightforward: low latency for the real-time inference path, strong auditability for our compliance team, and a clear runbook for cutover. we have a 12-week runway to pilot — hoping to get a working pilot by mid-november.

[00:45] Maya Patel: awesome. that's helpful. timeline wise mid-november is tight but doable. we've seen similar customers go from staging to pilot in 3–4 weeks when infra is ready. quick question — are you thinking hosted first or do you want private/dedicated out of the gate?

[01:05] Samir Patel: we'd prefer hosted to get moving faster. but we do have an internal latency SLO: p95 under 150ms for the interactive flows. also we'll need encryption keys under our control — KMS integration or HSM.

[01:28] Jordan Kim: okay good. hosted-first with customer-managed keys is a pattern we support — Redwood can integrate with your cloud KMS or with customer-supplied HSM via our private deployment options later. small note: p95 includes network hop time if you go cross-region, so we'll want the service in the same region and VPC peering.

[01:50] Priya Nair: for the ML side the main quality metric is answer accuracy on our prompt set. we have three canonical prompts — we'll share them after this call. also caching behavior is important; we asked about prefix caching in the doc but want to validate it with our conversational flows.

[02:12] Maya Patel: perfect, priya. yes please upload the prompts — that'll help Jordan craft the batch/caching recommendations. Jordan, can you speak to caching and batching tradeoffs briefly?

[02:34] Jordan Kim: sure. so we have continuous-batch and prefix/KV cache. for low-latency interactive usage, prefix caching cuts token work for repeated contexts; continuous batching helps throughput but can add a bit of latency depending on the batching window. Our recommendation: for the pilot keep batching conservative (small batch window) and enable prefix caching for repetitive prompt patterns; we can tighten batching for cost later.

[03:03] Daniel Cho: on security, two things — SSO/SAML and audit logs retention. we need SAML with SCIM provisioning and 365-day activity logs. do you provide that?

[03:20] Avery Cole: yes, we support SAML and SCIM, and our enterprise auditing can retain logs per contract. i'll include the audit retention options in the packet. note that longer retention is part of an add-on.

[03:35] Elena Ruiz: good. can you also confirm network topology? Samir's concerned about opening public endpoints.

[03:45] Jordan Kim: absolutely — for hosted we offer private endpoints and VPC peering (or private link depending on cloud). you can keep traffic internal; only control-plane metadata crosses the public control plane unless you opt for our private deployment. we'll draw the topology in the workshop.

[04:08] Samir Patel: ok, i will share our VPC CIDR and the security team's contact. small point — we need to verify IP allowlists and firewall rules before peering.

[04:22] Maya Patel: noted; action: samir to share VPC CIDR and contact. we'll send a checklist.

[04:31] Priya Nair: another question on model variants — we currently run an in-house distilled model for some tasks and want to compare against the models in the redwood catalog. what's the best way to run A/B and measure regressions?

[04:50] Jordan Kim: we have per-route eval hooks — you can route 10% traffic to the Redwood model and 90% to your in-house, capture tokens and responses. Redwood Optimize can run quality regressions against your baseline prompt set and flag drops in accuracy. we'll include an eval config example in the runbook.

[05:12] Elena Ruiz: is that a paid feature?

[05:16] Maya Patel: Optimize is part of an add-on tier but for pilots we often include a lightweight eval config to help you validate. i'll put a note in the pricing packet.

[05:30] Speaker 1: (mumble) sorry can you repeat the KMS options?

[05:35] Maya Patel: yeah we support three options: use Redwood-managed keys (fastest), integrate your cloud KMS (AWS KMS/GCP KMS/Azure KeyVault) where keys are customer-controlled, or private on-prem HSM for air-gapped needs. for initial pilot, cloud KMS is the middle ground.

[05:58] Daniel Cho: cloud KMS sounds fine, but how do we handle key rotation and escrow?

[06:06] Jordan Kim: key rotation is supported — we can coordinate a rotation window. we don't escrow keys unless you're on private deployment; we keep key metadata but not plaintext. I'll include the KMS integration doc.

[06:22] Priya Nair: on observability — we need token-level cost breakdown and per-route latency dashboards. do you expose traces?

[06:33] Avery Cole: yes, console exposes token-level cost, latency percentiles, per-model breakdowns. we also provide tracing hooks to integrate with your datadog/newrelic; we'll include APM example scripts.

[06:52] Elena Ruiz: great. timeline: what are the milestones we should expect?

[06:58] Maya Patel: suggested milestones: week 0 (this call) — security packet and runbook template; week 1 — infra workshop with Jordan; week 2 — staging deploy and smoke tests; weeks 3–4 — pilot validations and metrics; week 6 — decision point to continue to prod/dedicated. does that align with your mid-november target?

[07:23] Elena Ruiz: yes that's fine. we'll aim to be ready for staging deploy within 10 days.

[07:30] Samir Patel: on the infra workshop — we want hands-on peering, a smoke test harness, and a basic load test simulating our 200rps traffic with burst to 600rps. can you support that?

[07:45] Jordan Kim: yes, we'll bring a test harness. for 200rps, hosted with autoscaling should be fine; if you see sustained peaks we'll propose dedicated capacity. note: cost delta for dedicated vs hosted is often worth it when sustained throughput reduces per-token overhead.

[08:10] Priya Nair: a quick callout — we have a sensitive dataset for evals, can we send redacted examples only?

[08:18] Maya Patel: absolutely. for privacy-sensitive evals, redactions are fine; also you can run the evals locally with our eval runner if you prefer.

[08:30] Daniel Cho: procurement question — do you support SOC2 documentation and a security questionnaire?

[08:37] Avery Cole: yes — we'll provide SOC2 Type II report, ISO attestation details, and an editable security questionnaire template.

[08:50] Elena Ruiz: what's the expected ramp for cost during pilot? we want a ballpark to budget.

[08:56] Maya Patel: i'll include pilot pricing scenarios in the packet — rough estimate depends on token volume and model choice. for an interactive chat workload at 200rps with our medium model, ballpark is X — i'll give concrete numbers in the follow-up.

[09:12] Speaker 2: (crosstalk) do we need dedicated infra for p95 150ms?

[09:20] Jordan Kim: not necessarily. If your p95 target is 150ms including network, hosted in-region with small batch windows and prefix caching often meets that. If you need <100ms p95 or have strict data residency/KMS mandates, dedicated/private is the route. we'll validate with benchmarks in staging.

[09:44] Priya Nair: ok that helps. can we also talk about feature flags? we might want to roll back quickly if quality drops.

[09:52] Maya Patel: yes — runbook will include canary and rollback steps; we support route-level fallback to a lower-cost model or to your in-house endpoint. automatic fallback policies can be set per-route.

[10:05] Elena Ruiz: great. what else for the runbook?

[10:08] Jordan Kim: key runbook sections: prep (VPC, SSO, KMS), deploy (staging steps, config), smoke tests (latency, correctness), observability (dashboards and alerts), rollback (traffic routing and thresholds), contacts (on-call and escalation).

[10:28] Maya Patel: i'll attach the runbook template after the call. quick note — we'd like to do the infra workshop next wednesday (2026-10-28) at 10am PT. Jordan, any conflict?

[10:40] Jordan Kim: good for me. Samir?

[10:43] Samir Patel: tentative yes, i'll confirm with security calendar.

[10:48] Elena Ruiz: sounds good. one more question — how are errors and rate limits surfaced to our app? we want graceful degradation.

[10:56] Jordan Kim: we return structured error codes; runbook will include retry/backoff patterns and a sample client middleware that implements graceful fallback to a cached response or an alternate model.

[11:12] Daniel Cho: any GDPR/data residency concerns for our EU customers?

[11:18] Maya Patel: we have region-specific hosting and can ensure inference region is EU for EU traffic; also we can configure data retention policies per-tenant. i'll include data residency notes.

[11:30] Priya Nair: last practical item — do you have a sample smoke test we can run locally?

[11:36] Jordan Kim: yes, i'll upload a lightweight harness (python scripts) and a dockerized load generator. we'll put links in the workshop invite.

[11:50] Maya Patel: ok wrapping up — recap: we'll send SSO/KMS/security packet and runbook template by friday (2026-10-22); jordan will schedule infra workshop and test harness for 2026-10-28; priya will upload sample prompts and baseline metrics; samir to share VPC details. next sync after workshop to confirm staging deploy date.

[12:12] Elena Ruiz: perfect. thanks everyone. excited to get started.

[12:18] Maya Patel: thanks all — we'll follow up with notes and action items.

[12:22] (meeting ends)

Notes on transcription: occasional words unclear (speaker labels may be approximate), product names sometimes slightly altered (e.g., "Redwood Optimize" heard as "Redwood Optima" in a few places).
